utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good afternoon, Madam Registrar. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-PT, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. So let's go to the usual formality. I will be asking each of the accused whether they can follow the proceedings in their own language. I'll start with Vujadin Popovic. Good afternoon, to you, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Mr. Beara. The same question to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BEARA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can follow, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Beara, and good afternoon to you. Mr. Nikolic. Same question: Are you receiving interpretation in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Nikolic, and good afternoon to you too. Ljubomir Borovcanin, good afternoon to you. Can you follow the proceedings --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Your Honour, I can hear everything and understand everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, and good afternoon to you. You may sit down. Vinko Pandurevic, good afternoon to you. Can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Milan Gvero. Can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour Mr. President. I can follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gvero, and good afternoon to you, too. And finally, Mr. Miletic. Can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Miletic, and good afternoon to you too. Let's go to the appearances. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President and Your Honours. Peter McCloskey. Appearing with me, Julian Nicholls and Janet Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it there is no one behind the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey, and a very good afternoon to you and your team. So appearances for Vujadin Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Zoran Zivanovic, lead counsel, and Julie Condon, co-counsel for Vujadin Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. A very good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for Ljubisa Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is John Ostojic. I'm here today with Mr. Christopher Meek, our co-counsel, and our legal assistant Walter Prentice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ostojic, and good afternoon to you and you were team. Drago Nikolic. Appearances for Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Jelena Nikolic and Mr. Stephane Bourgon for Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A very good afternoon to you both, Madam Nikolic, and welcome. Appearances for Ljubomir Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Aleksandar Lazarevic, and here by my side is Mr. Miodrag Stojanovic. We represent Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Lazarevic, and good afternoon to you and your team, and I hope you will not be hiding behind the column for the rest of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances for Radivoje Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Natacha Ivanovic for General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam, and good afternoon to you. Appearances for Milan Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Dragan Krgovic and Natalie Wagner for General Milan Gvero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you both. And last but not least, appearances for Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you for the "not least," Your Honour, and good afternoon. At this table for Pandurevic are myself Peter Haynes, Djordje Sarapa, and our legal assistant Francesco Rindi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Haynes, and a very good afternoon to both of you -- to the three of you. So Madam Fauveau, are you going to be assisted or are you going to be alone in this case? I'm asking you because if you have any problems, if you have encountered problems and you need the Trial Chamber's assistance, I can assure you, as on previous occasions, you will find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you very much for asking this question. I'm currently in the process of negotiation about Nenad Petrusic, negotiations with the Registrar. A decision was taken, but it was not a positive decision because he doesn't speak the language of the Tribunal and he took part in another case in the Tribunal so the Registrar deemed that there was a conflict of interest. Then the Chamber decided that it was too exaggerated to say that it was a conflict of interest and the main problem was a language problem. I underwent negotiations with the Registrar in order to obtain counsel speaking B/C/S, which is absolutely essential for my case, because I speak the language but I speak Croatian, so I sometimes find it difficult to read documents in the Cyrillic alphabet. But I can't seem to be able to find an agreement with the Registrar. Furthermore, circumstances have been changing. Because even if the Registrar deemed that Mr. Petrusic was not possible because there was a conflict of interest he was appointed as a legal counsel. I stated that his duty would be to be in touch with my client whilst he was in -- still provisional release, and the Registrar said that it was possible and he was appointed as a member of my team. Furthermore, as far as I know, when the Prosecutor was contacted about this and the Prosecutor made written submissions saying that, according to them, there was no conflict of interest regarding Mr. Petrusic for him to be able to be part of this case. There is something else, and that is that at the time Mr. Krstic, who was the client of Mr. Petrusic, was on the list of witnesses of the Prosecutor, and that's not the case any more. And this is something that reduces the possibility of a conflict of interest. Unfortunately, today I received a rather unpleasant letter from the Registrar. I can't call it anything else than blackmail because I'm being told that if I don't appoint someone who complies with all the conditions set by the Registrar, then all the resources allocated to me will be stopped. I must say that I have tried my best to find somebody who is suitable. Unfortunately, there is no one on the 45 list who speaks B/C/S. I don't think that it's up to the Registrar to tell me you don't need anybody who speaks B/C/S. I really need a co-counsel who speaks B/C/S. I'm trilingual; I speak French, English, and B/C/S. Unfortunately in this case, that's the B/C/S language that I master the least because I'm used to the variant of the language that is -- that is spoken in Croatia. Any help coming from the Chamber would be extremely useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Please keep us informed about -- about further developments, and hopefully there will be some kind of agreement reached between now and when we start with the trial. In the meantime, I will try to find out exactly what is happening. Then you know that we can only intervene in a very limited extent, but there are instances when we can do something. We'll see after hearing the other side of the story. Thank you. So before proceeding any further, it's my great pleasure as Presiding Judge in this trial to welcome Judge Ole Bjorn Stole from Norway. I welcome him on behalf of the Trial Chamber, on behalf of Judge Kwon and Judge Prost. We've had already an opportunity to meet and discuss several matters. Judge Stole was sworn in earlier on this morning and he will be a valuable addition -- he is a valuable addition to the Trial Chamber in this -- in this complicated case. Let's start with the Pre-Trial Conference. And you would have already received a copy of the decision that we handed down this morning on the several motions that I referred to during the Status Conference that we held on the 6th of this month, motions challenging the second consolidated amended indictment. You will recall that the second consolidated amended indictment was filed by the Prosecution on the 14th of June. Then we had challenges to it by Accused Popovic, Pandurevic and Borovcanin. Relative motions challenging the indictment were filed on the 23rd and the 30th of June. There was a response, an integrated response from the Prosecution on the 3rd of July, and a further reply from Accused Borovcanin on the 4th of July. As we intimated to you during the Status Conference, we have succeeded in concluding -- coming to a decision which we handed down earlier on. Just want to make sure that everyone is aware of this and that you have all received a copy of it. Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Defence, is there any Defence team that has not? Okay. That's good. So I'm also informed - and I have a confirmation of it, actually - that as -- that the second consolidated amended indictment was duly translated by the CLSS and forwarded to each and every one of the accused, and I just want to make sure that I have -- that we have the correct information. If there is any one of the accused that has not received in B/C/S the second consolidated amended indictment, please speak out now. All right. So that confirms. So the first point we wish to make in the wake of the decision that we handed down this morning is that to us now all Rule 72 challenges to the second consolidated amended indictment have now been disposed of, and there will be no further Rule 72 objections or submissions to be filed. For all intents and purposes of law, then, we will and we are hereby declaring the second consolidated amended indictment to be the operative indictment in this case until such time as the Prosecution submits a new indictment in -- which would conform to what we decided earlier on this morning. As you know, we have in the decision itself fixed the 4th of -- of August for the filing of the revised consolidated amended indictment. We chose that day and not an earlier date because, as I will shortly be explaining in private session, we think that the Trial Chamber, but more particularly both of you, Prosecution and -- and Defence, will benefit from a clean and accurate indictment which would even go beyond what we decided earlier on this morning. Let's go, for a couple of minutes, into private session. I need to address something which I think can be dealt with in private session. It's not of public consumption. Let's --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you so much. One of the main conclusions we -- the decision -- our decision of this morning contains is that basically the second consolidated amended indictment does not contain any new charges. This means that all the accused that have already entered pleas against all the charges applicable to them as contained in the 11th November indictment during the Status Conference of the 4th of April and that of the 6th of July do not have to re-enter pleas. The pleas remain as they are. That applies to all the accused bar one, and that's Borovcanin. And I will try to explain the accused Borovcanin's position as it emerges now in the wake of this morning's decision. You will recall that way back in April Mr. Borovcanin had pleaded -- entered a plea of not guilty to all counts except count 2. The reason for not entering a plea to the charges contained in count 2 was, as put by Mr. Lazarevic at the time, that it was not clear from the second consolidated amended indictment that he was being indicted or amongst the indictees under count 2. That matter has now been resolved by our decision, and the decision is that he is indicted under count 2 of the second consolidated amended indictment. At the time when he refused to enter a plea on count 2, we decided to postpone his entering a plea till the matter was ultimately resolved by a decision of the Trial Chamber. Therefore, our conclusion is that, after this morning's decision, he now is in a position to enter a plea, and this for -- for the purposes of this exercise, this is not a further initial appearance. We're not talking of a new charge, it's just a clarification that has been established by our decision and, therefore, Mr. Borovcanin will be very shortly called upon to enter his plea on count 2 today. However, our decision is that he also needs to enter a plea or re-enter a plea in relation to count 1 of the second consolidated amended indictment. Let me explain on behalf of the Trial Chamber the position. When in -- earlier on, Mr. Borovcanin pleaded not guilty to count 1, count 1 was limited to aiding and abetting genocide. In our decision of the 31st May, we -- we ordered or we directed the Prosecution to clarify under which form or forms of responsibility Mr. Borovcanin was being charged under count 1. The Prosecution, as you will recall, did so by deleting the phrase "limited to aiding and abetting genocide," and in our decision which we handed down this morning, we held that the resulting language of count 1 removes the ambiguity in relation to Mr. Borovcanin's alleged responsibility for genocide and appropriately reflects now the fact that he's charged now, as he was in the consolidated amended indictment, with participation in the joint criminal enterprise to commit genocide. So that having been re-established, basically, and with the deletion of the words "limited to aiding and abetting genocide," he will now be required to re-enter a plea also in relation to -- to count 1. And I think before we move any further to the other items on the agenda for today's Pre-Trial Conference, we will proceed immediately with this matter. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will be asking your client very shortly -- I would like to see -- because if -- if you could at least for one moment exchange place with your colleague. And I don't mean to offend your colleague by any chance, but I think ... In the first place, do you require a short time to explain to your client the position in case he has not understood or has not followed what I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that Mr. Borovcanin understood very well what you are asking him to do. However, earlier this morning we were in the Detention Unit with Mr. Borovcanin, and while discussing this issue with him, we were not aware of the decision which was rendered later, and I became aware of it only some 30 minutes ago when I arrived here. So if I can ask for only five minutes of -- to confer with Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have got this option: We can -- you can do that during the first break, and we can postpone this. I think it will be easier, so that if you require more than five minutes, you will have the opportunity without us needing to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. I believe that it would be the best solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I -- please, security officers, one of you, whoever is in charge, needs to ensure that there will be the possibility of counsel to approach and have a chat with his client during the break. In other words, make the necessary arrangements. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. He will only be asked to enter a plea in relation to counts 1 and 2 and then we can proceed. So we'll come to this after the break, and I thank you for your cooperation, Mr. Lazarevic. And let me now address outstanding motions. There isn't much that I need to add to what we already discussed during the 6th July Status Conference, but there are some developments, and I think we need to address those developments. The day after we had the Status Conference, the Prosecution filed its consolidated reply and relation to the various responses that were filed by the various Defence teams on the adjudicated facts, on the Prosecution motion for -- on adjudicated facts. There was one exception and that was Accused Beara. Two days ago - and we only received it yesterday, actually - Counsel Ostojic for Mr. Beara filed a motion for leave to file a delayed response to the Prosecution motion, as well as a copy of the response that he seeks leave to file. These filings exceed the deadline which was set by the Trial Chamber which was of the 30th of June. It exceeds by 11 days. So before we eventually proceed to hand down our decision of whether to grant leave or not, we wish to have a quick oral response by the Prosecution whether they take a position on this, on the request for leave, basically, first, and then we'll discuss something else afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we'll take no position at this time, this early in the programme. I'm sure this -- I trust this won't be a common occurrence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. No. We anticipate that too. That being the case, we can indicate that we are inclined to grant the motion. The same applies when I later refer to a second motion of Mr. Ostojic relating to the Rule 92 bis. Would you be requiring time to file a response to both Defence motions, both in relation to the adjudicated facts and 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just -- I think the usual time would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So I think we can dispose of that in due course. In any case, the decisions on both the adjudicated facts motion and the Rule 92 bis motion are not to be expected before the recess. So you will have the regular time for filing of your responses. That's all I had to state in relation to the outstanding motion relating to the proposed judicial notice of adjudicated facts. Are there any further submissions that you, Mr. McCloskey, or any one of the Defence teams would like to make at this stage? And those will be considered to be final submissions, of course without prejudice to the responses that you will be filing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, as, I think we spoke briefly last time, with the new case coming out of Rwanda, we've been reading that to determine whether it's appropriate, and we would like to file something on that, hopefully within a week because of the -- and we've been trying but, as you can see, things keep happening. But I think we should be in a position that we can file something within about a week on that, just to draw the parties' attention to that new case and how it may affect the outstanding motion, as well as the Oric judgement we believe has some relevance. We're looking at that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. So the position hasn't changed, actually, from what it was on the 6th of July with the exception that you anticipate within a week you will be able to produce something. I take it there are no further comments. Then there is the other outstanding motion that I have already referred to. That's the Prosecution motion for admission of several 92 bis statements. I've dealt with the motion for leave to file a delayed response on behalf of Mr. Beara. That will be decided tomorrow. There was the issue that we raised during the Status Conference relating to some of the Rule 92 bis statements that you were proposing, namely, that there was reference in there to several exhibits that were used during the testimony that were not included in the DVD or CD-ROM that was provided, and that we had made it clear that in our opinion we could evaluate, fully evaluate the prior testimony of the proposed Rule 92 bis witnesses if we were able to see these exhibits. And we asked you to provide us a list, at least with cross-references, or to provide us directly with a new DVD which would include those exhibits. What's the latest on this, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're halfway through that, and I'm told that we can get you the entire fished product by the 20th. Again, in about a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much. Any remarks from the Defence bench? Thank you. Something that we have worked intensively upon, and which we are in the process of finalising is the matter relating to the 18th May Prosecution motion for protective measures, which is the only motion for protective measures filed so far. You will recall that there were Defence responses filed on 1st and the 2nd of June to which the Prosecution then filed a consolidated reply on the 8th of June. We are in the process of finalising our decision, as stated. What we would like to know from you, Mr. McCloskey, and if necessary we will go into private session for this purpose, is whether, in addition to the information that you provide in your motion relative to each one of the persons for whom you seek protective measures, whether in addition to that information, you have other information that can make our task easier, which would enable us to evaluate better whether you really deserve to have your motion for protective measures accepted; and if yes, to what extent. I mean, we find that compared to several other motions that we have come across in our work here in this Tribunal over the years that they are pretty much laconic compared to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sure there is more information. We of course try to make your job as easy as possible, but as you know, this is an ongoing process. Security sometimes ebbs and flows, depending on the situation on the ground, and I know there's at least a couple of cases where that has happened, and -- but they are all very individual, and if we had a moment or some time to look into each individual case, we could provide individual information. If there is anything new that we can provide you, there isn't very many, so that shouldn't be too difficult. And we certainly will answer any questions. This is -- a lot of the time it's hard to anticipate where your concerns are, but that's what we're trying to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our concerns are if we are to decide - and we ultimately have to - decide on your motion, dispose of your motion, and you are pretty much specific as to what you request in your motion, then we are asking you whether you can provide us with more information. And if yes, how soon you can do that, because the -- the trial is on the doorstep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll go over that this afternoon and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If necessary, we will dedicate some time to it for tomorrow morning in private session, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That would be fine. I think we can get through it this afternoon if we adjourn early, or maybe earlier before too late, and we'll be ready to talk about it. These things do always adjust, so I'm sure we can adjust it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why we are asking, because when you filed the motion, it was 18th May. Now it's two months after. And as you said, ebbs and flows, and so we'll require some further information and then we can proceed with our decision. And then some good news -- I thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask Mr. McCloskey, I wonder whether you are in the position to tell us whether these five witnesses are the only ones for whom this kind of delayed disclosure would be sought on the part of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're not aware of anyone right now, Your Honour, though I think I did mention last time, just so everyone is aware, one member of our -- one person on our witness list was shot and killed recently and under unusual circumstances that we're not fully apprised of. So it is an ongoing concern, as I know it is for you too, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did any of these witnesses give evidence in another trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In some forms, yes. I can think of at least one that did provide in -- I think it came in as 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were they given this kind of protection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Delayed disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You haven't identified those things in your motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We should have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can provide us with a much clearer picture tomorrow, we hope. Thank you. So Madam Fauveau and Mr. Krgovic, we have disposed of your motion -- respective motions for temporary provisional release, which will become operative after we finish the opening session of the trial tomorrow. The understanding is that your clients will need to be back here not later than the 14th of August. You are aware of our decision, I suppose. Thank you. Let's deal with disclosure matters very quickly. We dealt with much of or most of the matters relating to disclosure during the 6th of July Status Conference. Mr. McCloskey, is the disclosure of all witness statements completed by now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's one witness we're working on and otherwise we're finished. I think there are a couple of translation issues, but we've practically got the translation issues down to a bear minimum, so we're very close to the translation issues, and we have one -- one other witness that we noticed we thought was on the list and was not, but we have his statements and that will be rectified very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Any remarks on this by -- yes, Madam Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we discussed this at the Status -- at the last Status Conference, and the situation is the same. No progress has been made with regard to disclosing 16 witness statements in the B/C/S language, and there are another 11 witness statements that were provided to other bodies in Republika Srpska, not to Prosecution investigators. This is documents that BH institutions obtained for investigations in front of the court in Sarajevo. And there's another important matter, important for the Defence. On a number of occasions we wanted our colleagues to assist us. We requested assistance from our colleagues so that the last two or three disclosures made via EDS in regard of the Srebrenica collection be placed on CD. 28th of June and 29th of June of this year, these are the dates concerned, and there are a lot of documents that would be important for the Defence, for all Defence teams. If we could get these documents on CD, we could then process and deal with all the documents in good time. Furthermore, Mr. Nikolic's defence has attempted, on a number of occasions at meetings that were held, to have a look at some of the original documents. However, so far we have been unable to reach an agreement with our colleagues, we have been unable to gain access to such documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey, Madam Nikolic has raised not one but quite a few issues. Do you wish to address these issues separately, one by one, starting with the last one perhaps where she is alleging lack of cooperation, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think she means that. We've been talking, we've been able to provide her with things. There's one original document that is an expert in the UK, and still working on it. We've told her that, and we're going to try to get it back. She's probably frustrated because it's in our expert's hands, but it will be here. I'm not aware of any other problem. Anything that we have she is welcome to have, and we're ready to go down to the evidence locker and get it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And about her request for a CD compilation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is against the original understanding of providing the material on a hard disk and that updates would go on the EDS. It becomes extremely difficult and burdensome for the team to put -- make individual CDs for -- for all the accused in this situation when it can be done --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If anything, it will be for just one and then they will burn copies. No one expects you to provide secretarial services for --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's safer for us that we give them to everyone because even with the hard disk, it got lost for a while, Your Honour, and we don't want that to become a problem, and that's what this -- there's been a massive investment into this EDS system and we've made many exceptions, and we'll continue to work with them, but knocking out CDs which are -- you have to search them individually, so that takes away from the whole. And the great advantage of having something that's a whole searchable, then you're not going to miss things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are there any further comments on this -- these issues? Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I am understanding what you're saying, but I'm not receiving interpretation in English, and I want to make sure that the accused are receiving interpretation in their own language. I'm still not receiving, or of course -- I'm not expecting interpretation of what I'm saying, but I'm -- could you please say something again in French, Madam Fauveau, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's coming through now.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I ask you not to continue but to start again, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour. Last time I mentioned the fact that we had not received all the witness statements on -- pursuant to Article 92 bis -- Rule 92 bis on the list of witnesses. I will not repeat the name of these witnesses in open session. This adversely affects us. We are not sure that we have received all the witness statements currently in the hands of the Prosecutor of all the witnesses that will be called to testify. The witness statements are public and relate to Karadzic and Mladic. The counsel can access these testimonies because one can find the transcripts on the internet in English or in French; however, we cannot access a B/C/S version. I'm fully aware of the fact that the transcripts are not being translated, but the Prosecutor should nevertheless hand over the audiotapes of this testimony. We would also like to make sure that the Prosecutor has handed over all the witness statements. This would otherwise hinder the preparation of the Defence team and the preparation for this trial. We would like to make sure that before the testimony of the witness another witness statement has been provided to the Prosecutor several years beforehand, and this, of course, would delay the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Again there are several issues involved. Let's start with the easiest, the simplest one. I mean, we all know that testimonies here, or transcripts of evidence, is in what we see on the screen in English, and -- and if the original testimony is in B/C/S, then it is recoverable. It's available on tape. Is there any particular difficulty on your part in providing the taped version of these testimonies, because I wouldn't imagine the existence of such difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: None. And this is -- again, we have a very good relationship with Ms. Fauveau, and had we heard about her specific issues, we would deal with them. This is the first time I'm hearing of specific issues, and we're endeavouring to dig up as many, as -- all that we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. McCloskey. The other point raised by Madam Fauveau is in her considered opinion not all 92 bis statements have been made available. Do you accept that -- that that is the position, or do you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Given the complexity of hiding places for statements, that could be very well true. If she will help us look or identify which witnesses she's talking about, we will endeavour to search, as we have with her, and I invite all others to assist us in that process. We're doing a pretty good job, and I think they'll find in the previous two trials we did a very good job. So we'll continue. Give us a hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it stands to reason, Madam Fauveau, that you need to be more specific, not now and not in open session in any case, as regards your allegations, and it seems that Mr. McCloskey is giving us his word that he will attend to the various matters raised by you. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course I shall not quote the names of witnesses in open session. However, I would like to remind Mr. McCloskey that I reminded him of the three witnesses at the last Status Conference on the 6th of July in private session. So the names of these witnesses are to be found in the transcript in private session. I will of course contact the Prosecutor to remind him of the names of these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what you stated earlier on today, a few minutes ago, was it limited to those three persons, three names, or does it go beyond that? In other words, are there further statements of other persons that are still not available?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have difficulties in identifying the witnesses for which we have received no statement. We can only identify the witnesses if they have already previously testified in previous trials. There are three witnesses whom we have identified who have already testified in a trial. We would like a statement on the part of the Prosecutor stating that all the witnesses and witness statements have been disclosed to us, because we really can't identify them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I take it that the conclusion on this issue is that you will continue to liaise between yourselves and hopefully that will bear -- come to fruition. Mr. McCloskey, we mentioned last time the issue relating to Mr. Butler's, the military expert report. The only remaining aspect related to the translation of that report. Where do we stand?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The projected receipt date was today -- yesterday, sorry, and we have not received it today. But they're very good at those dates, and I would expect they'll be getting back to us very soon because we've, of course, asked them where it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And when are we to expect the -- the filing of all expert reports to be concluded?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we've -- we have a statement of General Smith that was -- is being taken, I think, right now as we speak, so it just -- again, in about seven days, and there -- I think an update of Helge Brunborg's demographics report, I was just speaking to them today, and they get, as you might imagine, data that comes in monthly related to identifications of people exhumed in Srebrenica, and they would like to update the report, and they said that they can provide me with an updated report in October because they're working on the -- two other cases, one that's in trial and one that's set for trial. But that is really an update and it's not a significant -- in some respects a significant issue. It doesn't change much, just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you so much, Mr. McCloskey. Are there any other remarks or matters that you would like to raise in relation to disclosure? I see none. Agreed facts. Again I mentioned this last time during the Status Conference, resorting to some wishful thinking, hoping today we would meet today and have a whole list of agreed facts. We have got some agreed facts incorporated in some of the final briefs filed by some of the Defence teams, but not much to write home about, to be honest. Can I, without wasting much more time on this issue, enjoin you to, as much as possible between now and when we start with the evidentiary stage, to try and lessen the burden of everyone, including yourselves, your own burdens, respective burdens, by agreeing to what can be agreed upon. There may be hundreds of facts that you could easily agree upon and that would leave us more time for more substantial issues to be dealt with in this Tribunal. Do I have your word that you will make an additional effort to try and provide the Trial Chamber with a more reasonable and more comprehensive list of agreed facts? Silence reigns supreme. It's only Mr. Haynes that nodded twice. Thank you. Let's deal with the next matter in private session for just two minutes, three minutes. I have some information to relay to you. This is a matter we have always dealt with in private session so far.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Proofing chart I don't think we need to discuss. We've discussed that enough. In relation to opening statements, we come to one important issue. We raised -- yes, I know. We raised this matter during the last Status Conference. Mr. Bourgon was not here. We had a declaration from some but not all of the Defence teams that they will or will not be making opening statements following that by the Prosecution. It's important for us to know, because first we have to continue planning and case -- managing the case as best as we can. Secondly, following the opening statements, the Prosecution will be calling their own -- their first witness, and they need to know whether that will be today or tomorrow, I mean basically. So I saw you standing, Mr. Bourgon. If you have any statement to make, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I meant to address the issue of the proofing chart. That's why I got up at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. President, we do believe that the issue of the proofing chart must be raised at this time at this Pre-Trial Conference, and I'd like to make a few observations in respect of the proofing chart. Granted, Mr. President, the proofing chart which was filed by the Prosecution, or parts thereof, was done so at the Chamber's request and was done so also according to the instructions that were issued by the Trial Chamber, and we -- of course we understand that the primary use of the proofing chart is for the benefit of the Trial Chamber and that the requirements are set in this regard. There is, however, a secondary use to the proofing chart and that is the use that the Defence will make of this chart, and we believe that the document filed so far by the Prosecution is, unfortunately, not much of assistance for the purposes of the Defence. Practically speaking, Mr. President, we would like to see, from a Defence point of view, we would like to have a chart that can be read by a witness, which is something that cannot be done with the product that we have been served with at this time. That is, Mr. President, for each witness, what the Defence is interested in getting is something that is rather quite simple. Simply, we'd like to have for each witness the following information divided into three parts: First, we'd like to know every single piece of material that is in the possession of the Prosecution with respect to a witness that will testify; that is, information that is provided by the witness, whether it is a statement, whether it is an interview, whether it is a so-called information report or previous testimony, as well, of course, as any document or potential exhibit that was given to the Prosecution by this witness. Now, that's the first part. Once we know exactly what the Prosecution has, what is this material, then we can prepare for that witness, and that is the most important part from the Defence point of view. The second part, of course, was what, I guess, matches the Trial Chamber's concerns, is that of the exhibits, is somehow matching the exhibits with the testimonies or with the witnesses. In our view, Mr. President, it would be much easier if for each witness we would simply get the list of exhibits first that will be used with the witness. So quite simply, the numbers of the exhibits that the Prosecution intends to show and use during the testimony of the witness; and the second part is, of course, documents that will not be used with the witness but are relevant to what the witness is bringing to this trial. The third part would then be, of course, because we imagine that there will be some orphan documents, or documents that cannot be matched to any witness, and for these documents the Prosecution should provide, in our view, Mr. President, the information that says what is the relevance of the document to the Prosecution's case. In this regard, then we'll be able to argue as to whether these documents are admissible in the first place. So in summary with the proofing chart, what we've received so far, in our view, is very complicated and very difficult to use. We would prefer to have a three parts document including, one, list of witnesses; two, for each witnesses, the material in the possession of the Prosecution, the exhibits that will be used, the exhibits that will not be used but are relevant; and then information related to -- relating to the relevance of the orphan documents that cannot be matched with each witnesses. We believe, Mr. President, that such a document or such a proofing chart would be of great assistance to the Defence, but not only to the Defence but really to the running of this trial, so that when a witness comes before the Trial Chamber, everybody knows what this witness will bring, what will be used, and then we can move much more quickly with each witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Any remarks, Mr. McCloskey? I assure you, Mr. Bourgon, that we tried to simplify the idea of a proofing chart as much as we could. The alternative would have presented you with a much vaster but also much more complicated proofing chart. Some of the matters that you raised are quite valid. Of course, however, you have -- I can anticipate you, some of the issues will be dealt with later on as we proceed, and indicate what our requirements will be as we go along from basically from one week to the other, from one month to the other, but also from one week to the other, and I think those will address some of your concerns. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to respond briefly. Most of what Mr. Bourgon has said is, I think, the normal preparation of any case. It's been delayed a bit with the proofing chart, I have to tell you, because I would -- my mind works similarly to the way his does, and we're endeavouring to do just that. In fact, of course, there's already a witness list, and it's -- as I've told him, it's in a rough order but put Butler way back, and we'll have rules related to the exhibits that will be used for each witness, how many hours or days beforehand, so they'll be able to see those. And as for documents that are relevant to that witness that the Defence may be interested in, well, that's his work. We'll of course help him, point out any Rule 68. We're also assisting the Defence with its vast amount of documents by trying to give them indexes by date, by name, by subject, so that it's not just a mass of documents, so that they'll be in a similar position as we are when it comes to trying to figure out what might be good for cross-examination. And so I think that should largely settle it, and we'll continue to work on both things. I'm -- what I am endeavouring to work on for all of us is a binder with each accused and with the key photographs, video, intercept, statements and evidence. There is not, you know, ten binders for each accused. It will be small and this will be the most direct evidence, which I think in the early stages is very helpful. And that's one of the projects we're working on as well as your project and Mr. Bourgon's project.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let me try to sum it up and close on this matter as soon as possible. We decided to extend the time limit for the Prosecution to file the definitive proofing chart precisely because we could see that the Prosecution was not trying to shy away from or avoiding from making available the information that would be required, and we realised that the work involved was enormous, and we had proof of that when we got the first consignment, sort of. That's indicative. As we go along, I think we will need more information. We'll be able to make an assessment as we go along. If there are gaps to be filled, I'm sure we can fill them as we go along. But I don't think we should endeavour at this stage to devise a -- the perfect proofing chart, because that would only be possible to provide when this case is over and not before it starts. It is problematic. I mean, it presents a lot of problems, such a proofing, and we tried to cut down on what we -- on templates that we had early on to make it feasible, to make it possible. All right? Yes, I saw you standing, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just very briefly. As far as the proofing chart is concerned, it's Annex B of the proofing chart. You ruled, ordered that the Prosecutor should identify the witnesses and match it with the paragraph in the indictment, and you said that this should apply to all the accused. My client and Mr. Gvero find themselves in a particular situation because they are not charged on all counts and not all paragraphs concern them. The Prosecutor excluded paragraph 27 to 30 and the paragraphs relating to Miletic and Gvero. But if we look at the proofing chart, alongside the name of General Miletic and Mr. Gvero and the names of the witnesses, we can see that paragraphs 27, 28, 29 and 30 have also been included for these two accused. I think you had stated that it was important to identify the paragraph and match it with indictee. I would like the Prosecutor to clarify this, please. In addition, we spent a lot of the Pre-Trial Conference talking about the charges for which Gvero and Miletic are indicted for. I think the indictment is now sufficiently clear, but as far as pre-trial brief and the proofing chart are concerned, we don't have enough indications. We don't know what kind of evidence is going to be used against the accused. We would like to be able to prepare our Defence case as best as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not preempt certain issues. The proofing chart that has been filed to now is a partial one, covering only a limited period of time, and that may explain several of the queries that you made. On the other issue relating to the application vis-a-vis your clients, your respective clients - Mr. Krgovic too - relating to paragraphs 27, 28, 29 and -- 27 to 30, I don't have an answer, of course, unless it's the usual problem with cut and paste. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we can argue over this proofing chart and how accurate or applicable it is, as we will. I would prefer that we do that with the indictment, frankly. But I think the problem she's referring to is that Gvero and Miletic have not been charged with the murder operation. It was the Prosecutor's discretion which to charge them with, and that may have created the issue she's referring to. You will hear lots of evidence of their possible knowledge and involvement in all the events charged, but it was the discretion to have this as targeted as possible that has led to this situation and the charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But anyway, look into it a little bit further. I think deserves to be dealt with. I think -- yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour, but I must say that it is this position of the Prosecutor which upsets me. We need to know what the charges are in legal terms but in factual terms against our client, and we still don't know this. We have not asked for the joinder of cases. The accused here present must have the same right as if they were being tried individually. If we proceed this way, if we don't know what the charges are, if we don't know what facts the charges are based on, we would ask a severance of charges, of trials here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not create a storm in a teacup. Everyone is a lawyer here, and I suppose I don't need to say much more. Your clients are not being charged under the proofing chart, Madam Fauveau, they are being charged under the consolidated indictment, as is and as finally determined this morning in our decision. So I don't think your concerns that they may be charged with additional crimes because of what may be rightly or wrongly included in the proofing chart should be a legitimate concern of yours. I think we need to have a break now, a 30-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, we had arrived at opening statements before we reverted to proofing charts. So, so far, following the last Status Conference, the indications that I have -- that we have are the following: First that Mr. Zivanovic -- Mr. Haynes indicated that he has no intention to make an opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We shan't have an opening statement after Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We shan't have opening statement after the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So far I've got declarations from Mr. Meek on behalf of Mr. Ostojic, saying that Mr. Ostojic is planning to make an opening statement. Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Do you have an idea of the duration of your opening statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not at this time, I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When will you be able to come forward with an indication of the duration?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There's two factors that would play in determining my length and that is, one, how long the Prosecution gives their opening statement, which I'm not sure exactly how long they'll be, but it will be less than theirs. And secondly, I'm in the process of still drafting it and outlining it, so I should know in the next -- by the 10th of August, I would assume I would know definitively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We also need to know, and the Prosecution needs to know. I will soon be asking the Prosecution for an estimated time for their opening statement, but I understand from what you had stated earlier that you're thinking of one session or two sessions. Let's start from you, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe I want to have the option of taking a -- our normal court day, which is, what, two sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it may be shorter. It wasn't that long last time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what you indicated. You indicated a minimum of about three hours. That's what you had indicated. So let's assume for the time being that Prosecution will have one day, or one sitting day, for their opening statement. Now, Mr. Ostojic, you need to tell us, more or less, how long you will expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you right now I expect it should be no more than two hours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So Mr. Ostojic, two hours. Mr. Zivanovic and Mr. Haynes have already indicated that they will not be making any opening statements. I need a confirmation of that. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear -- listen, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I will repeat it. I need a confirmation from you that you will not be making an opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, Madam Nikolic, you reserved to tell us later on, and that's today. Time up now?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's your intention as regards opening statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our intention is to give an opening statement. It will go on until 3.00 at the latest, but we will confirm all the details, but we'll need no more than three hours, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I found the transcript saying --

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're confirming the duration of the opening statement. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, Madam. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is not our intention to give an opening statement after the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we won't be making an opening statement, and the accused won't be making any opening statement pursuant to Rule 88 bis [as interpreted]. No one will be making an opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we won't be making an opening statement pursuant to Rule 84, but my client will make a statement pursuant to Rule 84 bis, but he will need no more than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's it now. I had intention -- I had intended to deal first with your opening statements and then whether your respective clients would like to make statements. Let's go through the list again. Mr. Zivanovic, you will not be making an opening statement, but would your -- will your client Mr. Popovic be making a statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He will not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ostojic, are you aware whether Mr. Beara would wish to make a statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I am aware and he will not at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Madam Nikolic, same question to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Our client's position is identical; he won't be making a statement pursuant to Rule 84 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. Mr. Borovcanin will not be making an opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau-Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I've already said that my client won't be making an opening statement. I just want to add there's a translation error that's been made. It concerns Rule 84 bis and the transcript says Rule 88 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for pointing that out, Madam. And Mr. Haynes, Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your Honour, he will not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So as I see it, we require one -- assuming one full day for your opening statement and one and a half days for the two opening statements, one by Mr. Ostojic, one by Madam Nikolic, and the statement that Mr. Gvero intends to make. So we will make provision for those. And you, Mr. McCloskey, you have prior notice that basically the first three days of trial will be dedicated to these opening statements, and then you can follow suit with the first witness immediately after.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we begin Monday, so three days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and you need to have a witness here --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thursday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's up to you. We will interfere the least possible with how you wish to proceed with the list of witnesses. I mean, it's up to you whether to bring Mr. X before Mr. Y or change, provided the Defence and the Trial Chamber are given adequate pre-notice, okay, adequate notice of that. So -- all right. We have sorted that out, and I thank you so much for being so cooperative. Mr. Lazarevic, earlier on I asked you and you replied that you needed some time to consult with Mr. Borovcanin. Shall we proceed with his pleas now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I had the opportunity to discuss this with Mr. Borovcanin during the break and he's ready to enter pleas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much. I thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Borovcanin, you may remain seated for the time being and then when I ask you to stand up, please do so. I want to make sure, but already we have an indication from Mr. Lazarevic that you have -- you have, first of all, received a copy of the consolidated amended indictment in your own language or in a language that you can understand. That's the first. Secondly, I want to know whether you have read it. Thirdly, I want to know whether you understand the import of the two counts, counts 1 and 2, as that you will be asked to enter a plea upon, and lastly whether you are prepared to enter a plea today. So let's take them one by one. Have you received a copy of the indictment in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have received a copy the indictment in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that you have had also time and opportunity to discuss the indictment and your prospective plea with your counsel? You've had the facility, the possibility to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you understand the import, the legal significance of the two counts that you will be asked to enter a plea upon today; count 1 and count 2?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And are you prepared to enter a plea today?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovcanin. According to our Statute and our Rules, you have a right to have these, count 1 and count 2, read out to you in their entirety. There's no point in even referring to reading the entire indictment again because we are dealing just with counts 1 and 2. Do you wish to have these two counts read out to you in their entirety or do you waive this right and we can proceed with the relative questions as to what you wish -- what plea you wish to enter?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I waive the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Borovcanin. What I will be doing is that I will proceed with asking you whether you -- what -- what plea you wish to enter to each of these two counts. I will start with count 1. Your answer should be guilty or not guilty. You also have the right to remain silent, in which case we will enter a plea on your behalf, a plea of not guilty on your behalf. Count 1 of the indictment as it now stands charges you with genocide, punishable under Articles 4, 3(A), 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of this Tribunal. How do you wish to plead to this count 1 of the indictment, that is charge of genocide; guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Borovcanin. And count 2 charges you with conspiracy to commit genocide which is punishable under Articles 4, 3(B) and 7 (1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. How do you wish to plead to this count 2 of conspiracy to commit genocide; guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am convinced that I am not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Borovcanin. You may sit down. Madam Registrar, could you please enter into the records of the case that Mr. Borovcanin has pleaded not guilty to both count 1 and count 2 of the second consolidated amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. So you know that tomorrow there will be the official start of the trial, and we have already agreed that opening statements will be -- start on the 21st of August. I don't -- I think you need to understand that there are no changes anticipated to that, and I think we can, because of that, proceed to discuss now the conduct of trial, and there are very -- various issues that I on behalf of the Trial Chamber would like to raise. Let me introduce this subject very briefly as follows: Practically every counsel sitting in this courtroom has had vast previous experience in other cases before this Tribunal. You also know that it has been the practice until now in various, although not in every Trial Chamber, to proceed with annunciation and enunciation of guiding principles relating to presentation of evidence, admission of evidence, conduct during the trial. It is well charted territory, and we've discussed it amongst ourselves, but you are all pretty much aware of what the applicable rules and practice of this Tribunal have been because you've been working here for quite a few years. So we came to the conclusion that we would be almost offending your intelligence if we were to repeat once more in this -- now in this trial, guidelines that you are already very much familiar with. There are some issues, however, that are particular to a megatrial like this that need to be addressed, and of course we have no right to take for granted that issues that have been dealt with previously in these standard guidelines may not be the subject of queries on your part or that you may not require further elucidation on some of them, or guidance, guidance on some issues that we may not have anticipated. One of the first things that I wish to deal with is that the estimated time of -- for the completion of the Prosecution case partly depends on what our decisions on the Rule 92 bis and adjudicated facts motion will be, but then it also depends on the length of each examination-in-chief and also and particularly so on the length of the cross-examination considering that we have seven Defence teams now. There is another related aspect to this issue that we will be very shortly discussing, and that is that before the Prosecution is in a position to know when to call the next witness and the next witness and for us to be able to plan ahead, we would need to know what time would be required for the cross-examination of each and every witness. This is something which is so obvious but so fundamental that it requires that we deal with it today in the first place, and the beacon that shows us the way is more or less the decision that has been handed down by the Appeals Chamber recently in the Prlic appeal, namely that the rule of the thumb should be flexibility. So let's start with the Prosecution. Of course you will be planning ahead, and your plans will depend on several contingencies over which sometimes you have control, sometimes you don't. What we require from you, and we'll also, of course, obviously ask for your feedback on this, is that on a weekly basis, on an ongoing basis too, but on a weekly basis, on a particular day to be established now of the week, you will need to provide the Defence teams and the Trial Chamber with the witnesses you intend to bring forward. Now, initially let's start, because I'm dealing with a weekly document. I should have started with the monthly document. That's where you should start. Basically you should give an indication of what your intentions are for the next month, for the following month as we go along. That would indicate the names of the witnesses, reference maybe also to the proofing chart as to -- or any developments as to the subject matters that they will be dealing with, estimated -- estimated time required by the Prosecution for examination-in-chief for -- or direct, as you call it in your country. That would provide enough information for the Defence teams to be able to come back on their part with an estimate of how much time they require for cross-examination. Now, where flexibility comes in is obviously because there are some witnesses that will come forward that would testify only on matters that are of concern or that relate only to one or more of the accused. There are witnesses that will come forward that will testify on matters that directly involve all the accused. And therefore, we cannot establish a hard and fast rule as from now as to how much time will be required for cross-examination. We will have to deal on a case-by-case basis as we go along, both on the case of the Prosecution and in the case of the Defence, as we an along, depending on what the subject matter of the witness -- of the testimony will be. When we have that, and you also have an indication of what -- what the duration of the estimated cross-examination will be, or is, then obviously you can plan better, and that's where the weekly report or prognosis will come into the scene, into the picture. There you should already have an indication of how many witnesses you should bring in any particular week. The whole idea is that we don't only -- we do not only economise on time, but we also try to economise on the resources of the Tribunal. There is no point in having three witnesses here in town if the situation is such that you are going only to be able -- or that we are only going to be able to hear the testimony of one or two. So there is no point, as has happened in the past, of having one witness stay here an entire week or more. So we will need to do plenty of case management together. We are guaranteeing to you flexibility, but we are also expecting from both of you to be practical. We will use all the powers that we have as it may or as they may become necessary in the case of, for example, repetitive cross-examinations and so on and so forth. I mean, when we first met after the joinder of the various accused -- you remember, Mr. Bourgon, I had mentioned this, and I had enjoined you to start thinking about this. You will need as you go along to rally your resources and agree as to the best way of going about cross-examination of various witnesses. Where it will be necessary for each and everyone to have all the time required for cross-examination, you will get it. Where it is not necessary, we will need to determine or cut down as we feel should be the case. The same applies to the Prosecution, of course. The Prosecution will come forward and -- with an estimate of how much time they require for each witness. If it is necessary to discuss the matter with you, we'll discuss it in open court. I think our experience, those of us who have been here in the past, is that in these matters we've found cooperation -- cooperation when it was needed to cut down on time allocation, we could do so. Having introduced the subject the way I have, may I on behalf of the Trial Chamber ask you for an input. Later on, and precisely tomorrow, we hope to be able to come down with a set of guidelines that primarily would deal with such important issues like what I have just intimated now. So basically, we would like to hear your opinions on how -- on your part how the Prosecution should -- what facilities the Prosecution should have for a proper examination-in-chief, and the same with regard to cross-examination time that will need to be allocated. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we in the past have been able to provide reliable lists for about two weeks of witnesses, and we've been able to give reliable lists of exhibits to be used in those -- for those witnesses two days before any witness testified. And as for length of witnesses, we should for -- have hopefully reasonable time estimates. Many of the crime base people are pretty consistently two hours in direct. Mr. Butler and Mr. Ruez will take a while, and it's having this many -- well, Mr. Butler -- Mr. Ruez should take several -- four or five days, like he usually does. Mr. Butler will have more documents and we're going to have to really sort that out because we've tried to limit his testimony before, but we've had a limited number of individuals, so we've been able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we are interested in specific details now. What I'm interested in hearing from you particularly is the following: More or less I have projected a scenario whereby you come forward with a list of witnesses you have in mind of bringing along, bringing forward. That will be submitted to the Defence. The Defence teams will be required to coordinate, are expected to coordinate amongst themselves and then present you with a -- and of course the Trial Chamber, with an indication of the time required for cross-examination. That should then put you in a position to revise, if at all, your prognosis and say, okay, what -- the number of witnesses I anticipated to bring forward in the month of October, which was eight witnesses, has to now be cut down to four or five because of the anticipated -- then we come into play, we see what the situation is, whether it's the case of intervening or proceeding in accordance with your respective positions. So assuming that you are going to make available your list, your monthly prognosis on the, say, last day of the preceding month -- not the last day of the -- that you are going to present the Defence today with your prognosis for the two months ahead, basically, we're talking, because you would already have provided the list for the upcoming month. So once you have that, how much time you would require before you can -- how much time you would require to have a reply from the Defence team to enable you to provide a revised list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Realistically, Mr. President, I think we're all going to be so new that until we see this machine at work it's going to be very difficult to make any estimate based on what the Defence tells me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Let's deal with it in a practical manner. We will start with the testimony in the month of August. Now, I suggest that between now and a date which you will -- which you will yourself establish today, you will come forward with a list of witnesses that you intend to bring forward, which you already have, basically, for the months of August and September. Now, that list, please update it to see whether it has changed or whether it has remained the same by a date that you will be telling, saying now. You will have it at the disposal -- you'll make it available to the Defence teams with a copy to us. How much time would the Defence teams need, after mutual consultations amongst you, to decide on the estimated time of cross-examination for each of the intended witnesses? In other words, how much time do you need to provide the Prosecution -- if we say -- do you have any opinions on this? I mean, have you discussed it amongst yourselves?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make some submissions in relation to this? Your Honour, having read the decision of the Appeals Chamber in Prlic, perhaps can I seek some clarification from the Trial Chamber as to what the approach would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The approach is flexibility, I told you already. We will give you an indication too, very soon, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Perhaps what I'm specifically asking is that it seems that in Prlic, unless there is some agreement having been reached between Defence counsel, then the Trial Chamber will impose the 60 per cent rule, if I can refer to it as that. As far as our position is concerned on behalf of Mr. Popovic, I certainly haven't had the opportunity to discuss amongst my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but you are a newcomer. You've just arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I've just arrived, but I appreciate what Your Honour is saying insofar as the flexibility is concerned. Could I make this point on behalf of our client: No doubt there will be certain witnesses that are more significant in the case as against him than others. Cross-examination is difficult to estimate in the most ideal of circumstances, and it would be my position that with those witnesses that are of more significance to our case as we identify them, that I would certainly be more than happy to firstly engage in consultation with my learned friends as to what they expect in terms of cross-examination of that witness, and insofar as the Prosecution is concerned that as long as obviously sufficient notice is given as to when that witness is to be called I would certainly be in a position to indicate then, with as much clarity as I can, how long I expect to take with that witness. And rather than having the 60 per cent time allocation imposed, it would certainly be my preference to have the opportunity to have the flexibility amongst my co-counsel and obviously the flexibility with the Trial Chamber. So that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for your submission. Mr. Bourgon, you have a submission to make too?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We did briefly explore the topic in a meeting recently between Defence teams. Basically what you've just mentioned, first we'd like to say that we very much like the flexibility approach, and if the Chamber grants us that flexibility, we in return will grant the Trial Chamber all of our assistance and time in terms of limiting our cross-examination. That being said, in practical terms, for the first list of witnesses, we would propose the Prosecution to give us that list on the 4th of August, at the same time as the last indictment or the final indictment, for the list for August and September, and within five days we can return and provide both the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber with a total time of cross-examination, not by witness, simply to keep each of our trial strategies intact, but to have a total time. And then should the Trial Chamber decide to engage us and look into our submissions, then we'll be gladly then to explain further. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon.
