The message -- and I'm really appreciative, and I'm sure Judge Kwon and Judge Prost and Judge Stole will agree with me, I'm really appreciative that the words I said in the first days of -- after the joinder did not fall on deaf ears and that you have been proactive, and it's not just you, Mr. Bourgon, but it seems all the Defence teams. And that is a good signal that the Trial Chamber will expect good cooperation from you. The message that we need to send loud and clear is that when you have a trial of these dimensions -- of this dimension with seven Defence teams, good case management cannot allow for a situation to obtain which would not be conducive to a proper conduct and expeditious conduct of the trial. One such negative situation would be if we were to allow each and every one of you to go separately, when it comes to cross-examination, expecting -- expecting that there should be no imposition of any kind and that each one of you is not prepared or would not be prepared to consult or enter into consultation with other Defence teams for the purpose that I have explained earlier. So let's -- I see Mr. Haynes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your Honours, you've probably gleaned the Defence do cooperate with one another, and they cooperate with the Prosecution in this case, and Your Honour has correctly identified, as it were, the evils of trial mismanagement that we're seeking to avoid in any protocol that we establish. And I simply wondered whether I could make one practical suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your Honour was about to say that the Prosecution should provide by the end of every month its proposed list of witnesses for the following month, and given what Mr. Bourgon has said, it seems to me that there is a potential improvement to that suggestion, which is this: That the Prosecution should provide, say by the midpoint of every month, the witnesses that they propose to call for the following month. So they would provide by the 15th of September the witnesses they propose to call in October. (redacted) (redacted). But then seven days after that, the Defence should fill in their section on the form. And if the then completed, as it were, witness summaries lead the Prosecution to the inevitable conclusion that they've got too many or too few witnesses on the schedule for that month, it can be duly amended. I hope that is a helpful suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it is an extremely helpful suggestion, Mr. Haynes. Basically, however, it is predicated on the commitment also on the part of the totality of the Defence teams to meet the seven-day deadline, because otherwise the whole exercise will fall to pieces. Are there any further submissions that you would like to make? Should there be, for example, as a guiding principle, a ratio between the time that should, on principle, be available for cross-examination purposes in relation to the time taken by -- by the Prosecution in chief? In other words, for example, Ms. Condon mentioned the 60 per cent, et cetera. We are a larger number of Defence teams in this case to start with. Are there any submissions? Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's just a fairly significant matter. Can we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, and I think I anticipate what you are going to mention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With respect to your latest question, I would like to make the following suggestion: Simply that for the beginning of the trial not to set such a ratio and let's try and see how the Defence can cooperate with each other. It is very important for all of us, and we discussed this at our last meeting, that we have separate defences. There are separate accused, and each of the Defence team will be minding carefully the interest of their own clients. That is, of course, a basic for us. Now, that being said, we will try to cooperate and, as much as we can at the beginning, then we will suggest not to have any ratio, provide the Trial Chamber as well as the Prosecution with a total time for cross-examination for each witness, and this would then in turn allow the Trial Chamber to see if we are reasonable or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Yes. Let's make it clear, because I think we are speaking the same language.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically, we do anticipate the possibility that here comes a witness and all of a sudden two or three of you will have very much conflicting interest, or a situation where you have conflicting interests. At that point in time, expect the Trial Chamber to be not only flexible but also reasonable. And we expect you to be the same. And please do understand that these are not the problems. The problems are case management ones. We want to avoid by all means a situation whereby the message or the signal could be perceived -- transmitted or perceived that this is a sort of a free-for-all and, you know, there is absolutely no control with each Prosecution witness that comes forward, if he or she has been on the witness stand testifying for four hours, then every single Defence team will say we demand, we claim equal treatment, four hours each. I mean, because that will obviously be unacceptable. But it could well be the case that it becomes necessary on particular occasions. So I agree with you. We will need to play it by the ear and on a case-by-case basis, witness-by-witness basis, but what I'm asking you is the following: That the first step to avoid at all costs sending out an ambiguous message that flexibility is unlimited and without any kind of restraint, should it not be the case that we at least indicate to you and to the Prosecution that if considering that we are seven Defence teams here, and assuming a situation of normalcy, not a situation where there is a conflict of interest or where obviously it is imperative that each one of you goes ahead with a cross-examination, that there should be a beacon, a guideline, that the ratio should be, for example, as a guiding line one hour in chief, then it should be, for example, one hour, one and a half hours cross-examination time, two hours cross-examination. This is what we would like to hear from you. Then obviously the rule of the day, I mean the practice will be flexibility first and foremost but within a sort of self-imposed restraint that we are asking you to comment about. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the recent decision on that point was a good one. I think the one-on-one guideline is a very good rule of thumb, with flexibility, as you will be in the best position to recognise, but I think we all have been around enough that we can't really trust ourselves and our ability to hold ourselves back, especially when there's different interests. So I think discipline is going to be critical for all of us, and without a clear guideline and a clear rule, a flexible rule, we're going to get in trouble right off the bat. And we will be calling surviving witnesses, people that survived mass executions, that have testified twice before, some of them, and it will be very difficult if we don't have some pretty good guidelines from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. This is why, Mr. McCloskey, we are dealing with this in as exhaustive a manner as possible. And we are -- as you've said, we've been here long enough to know that sometimes anticipated time frames change during the course of the testimony itself. Sometimes it takes a shorter time, sometimes more time is required, and that's where flexibility becomes important. Now, there were instances where we obviously we have in the past, and also in the future, where we need to cut down, say no, Mr. Nicholls or Mr. McCloskey, you need to finish by the end of today and not any further, as Mr. Nicholls experienced in the previous trial, in Brdjanin, and the same will apply to the Defence. I mean, the anticipated time frame for the cross-examination may vary, depending on what the examination-in-chief reveals. I mean, sometimes there are questions that will not be asked. Sometimes there are new issues that come up that will require more time. So this is why we are saying there will be flexibility, that was -- is what we are aiming at. But we also need to have a guideline, an indication that ideally this is how it should be, and then we will move beyond or within, according to the exigencies of each particular evidence or -- or testimony or witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, no doubt I think I can understand you would go for a one-on-one guideline, but what would you suggest in case of witnesses whose direct evidence will be adduced in part or whole in writing? What would be your recommendation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A 92 bis witness, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 89(F). We have submitted a few 89(F) witnesses. That is not my choice, frankly, but I want -- because I want you to be able to hear the full nature of their evidence, but I think you do have to allow beyond the one-on-one principle if it's -- they need to be able to cross-examine on the material that's in the paper, and that would give -- you would give the Defence in that situation more than the ten minutes that you may have given the Prosecution. I have no objection. We would probably look at that 89(F) and try to compare him to a similar live witness. For example, if we had a survivor witness that we spent two hours going through the whole Orahovac case as opposed to an Orahovac witness that just said the basics and we relied on 89(F), they could take the two hours of what the former took if they felt they needed it. I don't think I would have any objection to that because of course you're right, they have to rebut the written evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Kwon, and I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Any further remarks or submissions on this issue? Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My earlier submission to Your Honours was to wait until we set that ratio. Setting the ratio now in the abstract is kind of difficult. Whether we say 1.5, as happened to one of my case I was in, or one-to-one, I think it's a bit early now to set a ratio without knowing how the dynamics of the trial will unfold. Now, what I'm able to tell you now, based on the conversations we've had together, if we provide the Prosecution within five days of the duration of each cross-examination in total by witness, the Trial Chamber has those witness summaries, the Prosecution can say, "I think this is too long," as the Trial Chamber can say, "I think the Defence is overdoing it." And after the first month we'll know right away where we are in kinds of ratio after one month. I simply suggest we wait a month for that ratio, and then should there be a need to say the Defence is overdoing it or the Defence is perfectly cooperating, then we'll be in a much better position in a month to set that ratio, given that we provide in five days the total time of cross-examination for each witness. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Any further submissions? Okay. So let me try and recapitulate. Ideally, forget the first batch. That's end of September. I think we have discussed that, and we can proceed along the lines suggested. You will provide the Defence teams not later than the 4th of August with an updated list of the witnesses you intend to bring forward during the month of August and September. Then within five days, let's say within a week, not later than a week - and I need your commitment on this - you will come back to the Prosecutor with your estimate of time required for cross-examination. On the basis of that, you will consider whether the list needs to be updated or not. That will cover us until the end of September. Now, as far as October and subsequent months are concerned, the suggestion is, and I think it's a practical one, that on the middle of September you will provide with the anticipated list of witnesses for the month of October. Within seven days, the Defence teams will feed you back with their estimate, and then we will work on that to have the updated list for the month of October. Similarly, mid-October you will provide for the month of November, and so on and so forth. Is that agreeable to the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. And just to clarify, I take it you're planning five days a week, one session? I don't think we have enough room for two sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. It's out of the question, because we are sharing this courtroom, Prlic trial and this trial, and there is no way we can sit. We can't sit in another courtroom, either of us. But I am coming to the question -- the other question that you have raised at the end of this -- of this part. So do I have the agreement of both sides to this arrangement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I check, Mr. McCloskey, whether, instead of producing a monthly list once a month, about updating the monthly list every week. That is another -- that would be possible as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm coming to that precisely, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's actually, as you know -- the way it turns out, that's a more realistic, in a sense, way because if we have a month list, (redacted) we find the various issues, and there's a little of juggling going on, we were pretty reliable for our two weeks ahead of time. After about two weeks, our list started getting a little bit not as credible, but we can update it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are two of a kind, you and Mr. Haynes. Yes. What Judge Kwon rightly raised is actually my next point. Moving from the monthly list, then we need to establish again another protocol which will deal with the presentation of testimony, of evidence on a weekly basis. Now, there we need to elaborate a little bit further. It's not just the list of the witnesses that you anticipate and the time frame you require, which I acknowledge can vary, especially after proofing of witnesses, but also an indication of the documents that you intend to use, and again I acknowledge that sometimes the documents that you will or not -- you will not be using depends very much on the outcome of the proofing. Now, there are various things that happen just before a witness starts testifying. The last phase is the proofing. Usually the practice, as far as I know it in other cases, has been that you would then provide the Defence teams with proofing -- proofing notes for their own purposes, especially if there are new issues that are going to be dealt with if the witness has made other statements that were not previously contained in -- elsewhere, and so on and so forth. I don't need to elaborate on that. What we require from you is disclosure of these proofing notes to the Defence teams in a timely fashion, and we are interested in two things. First, because it's only fair that it is done this way. Secondly, because if it is not done this way, we will come here and spend the first part of the morning exchanging accusations of bad faith, manoeuvring, and so on and so forth. So I think I have sent the message loud and clear. We will not be incorporating this in any written guideline, we are just enjoining you to adopt this as the practice. Similarly, I am sure that none of us will like a situation to obtain where we come here on any morning only to find out that the Defence team have just been informed a couple of hours before, if not a few minutes before, or by a note thrown in the respective letter boxes during the night that there will be new documents that will be used during the testimony. That would create again attrition and aggravation, and we should try to avoid the occurrence of such instances as much as possible. I know that it could happen and it will probably happen at times, but the important thing is that you try as a team, as an entire team, to avoid this happening as much as possible. What I want to make sure is that when we meet every morning or every afternoon here for a sitting to hear testimony of a particular witness, the Defence teams know beforehand well and in a timely fashion which documents you will be making use of. Then, of course, what happens later is -- you can decide not to make use of one or more documents, depending on how the examination-in-chief unfolds, but that's normal. So that's number two. I'm going, again, backwards up to -- so do you think that if I were to suggest that by not later than Thursday of each week you should provide the Defence teams with an anticipated layout of testimony and documents, time frames and everything anticipated for the following week, that is a deadline that you can reasonably meet from week after -- one week after the other?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't see any problem. We have to know that ourselves, with the only caveat that sometimes it takes us up to maybe two days before a witness, before we have a reasonable document list, but we will always -- we always manage to get it two days before any witness and we'll endeavour it make it sooner if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it changes, Mr. McCloskey. We all know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. As regards proofing notes, let's make one thing clear: That proofing notes that I referred to are required for the Defence teams, not for us. We don't want to see proofing notes unless and until there is a controversy on whether adequate disclosure of new information was given to the Defence team, and then maybe we need to have a look at what kind of proofing notes you have. But let's hope that need will never arise. It has arisen in Oric, it has arisen in quite a few cases. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can make one point: We, as you've seen from our witness list, there are many, many witnesses that are Bosnian Serb army or police officers, and many of those will be adverse to the interests of the Prosecution, perhaps, but have made statements before, and my experience in previous cases, there can be more change for those witnesses than there are others, so the proofing notes may be a little more complex. Hopefully not, but that's -- it's going to be more than I've ever put on in any case. So I wanted to just let you be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you so much. Are there any submissions you would like to make on this area that I've touched upon before I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I know we're not to the Defence case yet, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll be coming to that at the right time, Mr. McCloskey. I mean, they will get the same treatment. They will get the same treatment. They will eventually be required to meet the same requirements. So the -- summing it up: Thursday of every week you will furnish an updated list of witnesses, estimated time, matters that will be dealt with to make sure that nothing has changed, list of documents that will be used. Understanding is that it's granted that the list may change between that Thursday and the day when the witness arrives to give testimony. And as the day approaches for the testimony, then the question of the proofing notes and any changes in the list of documents or any other changes that are -- all right. I thank you. Now, something that we wish to raise now. Basically, the situation is that it seems that all the documentary evidence that so far, according to the 65 ter filings, the Prosecution intends to bring forward in the course of its case have been disclosed. It is quite possible that some of these documents may attract your attention more than others and that you may wish to challenge either the admissibility of these documents or you may be -- you may wish to challenge the authenticity of some of these documents. Some documents may be more important than others, but the more important they are, the more important it becomes for good case management that if you have reasons to object to those documents, you come forward with your objections the earliest possible. It's not correct, for example, let's say, that if one accused has made -- has released a suspect interview to the Prosecution and you as counsel wish to contest the admissibility of that statement or interview you would leave it until the very end of the trial to come forward with an objection after that that statement has been put to several witnesses and so on and so forth. So again, this is one area where we cannot impose a hard and fast rule because no hard and fast rule is envisaged in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence themselves, but it's an area where we are asking you to extend your cooperation to the best possible, to the best possible. If there are documents that you intend to contest -- to contest or to challenge, then the latest that you should aim at -- for the purpose of contesting them should be when that document first -- is first intended to be used with any particular witness and not then surprise the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution afterwards with -- with challenges late in the day. Any submissions on this? Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: None of us yet -- it's really an allied point rather than a submission directly to the point, but none of us yet for the Defence have been trained to use the e-court, but I wonder whether at this juncture, for those of us who have to manage our cases in particular in regard to documents, whether Your Honour would indicate at this stage whether this is a case that's conducted pure e-court or whether it is a case in which you would anticipate those who wanted to put documents into evidence providing you with hard copies as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We will be coming to that at the end of this Pre-Trial Conference, but I can anticipate, yes, and I can also anticipate that we have already taken -- made all the arrangements for each one of you to receive all the adequate training required before the opening statements. That will happen in the week starting on the 14th. In other words, we will be receiving training, our staff will be receiving training, and you will be receiving training, all of you, one team after the other. So I want to put your mind at rest on that. And the trial, yes, will be conducted on a pure E basis, however, we will require one hard copy of -- for the Trial Chamber, one hard copy of all the documents that will be tendered except when we say, no, we don't need this. So that's the position, but we'll come to that at a later stage. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I just wanted to reiterate the importance of what you had said for the Prosecution, because if there are going to be challenges, for example, to the authenticity of document collections, we have not anticipated that, and we have not put on perhaps the several witnesses that may be needed to -- to provide an authentication from any common law set-up. There is never in this case -- well, I should never say never, but there has never been the wholesale challenge to the authenticity of any collection. The occasional individual document has been challenged, and that's been relatively easy because it's come in through one individual as opposed to a search of a major brigade. Now, we are for the first time dealing with a collection that you're familiar with. I think I referred to it. It's the Drina Corps collection, and it managed to come into the possession of the Prosecutor under some rather interesting circumstances. We believe, from our review, it is valid and authentic, and if there is going to be a challenge, we need to know it now because that could involve lots more witnesses or -- or statements or however the Court would like us to do it. That same goes true of statements of accused if -- which we have two at this point. Any challenges, we would be needing to provide the basis that these statements were made under the rules and voluntarily. And without that challenge, it wouldn't be our intention to go through all that process in order to save time. So I appreciate any foreknowledge so that we can prepare for that. The individual document shouldn't be a problem, but the collections and large-scale things, witness statements, big pieces, we need to know now. Most systems require that to be up-front, but as you stated, our system --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our system doesn't address the problem, or the issue. What I can tell you is this: In previous cases in which I have been involved, when the issue of, for example, chain of custody or the manner in which the various documents or some collections came in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor was raised, then even though the Prosecution had not indicated any particular witness to testify on the chain of custody or on the way of recording the entry, receiving and entry and custody of these documents at your office, then of course the Prosecution was provided with all the opportunity, but again it was time-consuming. It was time-consuming. So, please, my appeal to you is as follows: Agreed there may be instances where information that will open your eyes and lead you to challenge the authenticity of a document or the admissibility of a document may not be available immediately at the start of the trial but may arrive later on. That is quite possible. It can happen. But we are not talking of those instances. What we're talking about is that now you have available already a list of all the documents that the Prosecution intends to adduce in this case. If you have reason to challenge any of those documents, please come forward with your objections at the earliest possible and do not leave that until later in the day. Any submissions? Any comments? Any disagreements with -- I see that even Mr. Ostojic agrees. Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. So we expect your cooperation -- your cooperation in this. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. At this time I would simply like to make a rapid submission regarding the admissibility of documents or the way in which a Chamber intends to proceed with regards to declaring or pronouncing on the admissibility of documents. Now, this is an issue that keeps up -- coming up in many trials and many different Trial Chambers have adopted a different mechanism. Now, I understand from what you have said earlier that you intend to proceed a la piece, or as the witness come, then the Chamber would declare the documents admissible at the end of the testimony of each witness. This is certainly the way we would prefer as the Defence team of Drago Nikolic, and we would like to know if that is indeed the case, that documents will be declared admissible only at the end of the testimony of each witness. The second question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. I didn't know you had a second --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Second question, Your Honour, is that of course this will leave a bunch of documents that have not been introduced through witnesses, what the Prosecution called the self-propelled documents, what I call the orphan documents. Now, what will be the procedure for -- to admit these documents on the record? Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's deal with the two aspects separately. Let's take the first one. The position that the Chamber, of course, can take it for granted that we have discussed the first part at length. The position that will be taken is as follows: If a particular document or if a particular collection of documents, for example, are challenged as inadmissible, then you will be asked to make submissions and we will come down with a decision as to whether they should be -- they are going to be admitted or not. The criteria that we will use will eventually be spelled out in the respective decision or decisions that we will hand out from time to time. As to the rest, if Prosecution comes tomorrow and seeks to tender this document, unless we hear any objection from any of the Defence teams, that document will be admitted. That document will be admitted. As to the others that are challenged, there will be a decision. And the decision may end up with marked for identification temporarily and then we will end up, at the end of the trial, during the deliberative stage, exercise, to decide what probative -- on the probative value and so on and so forth, but what we want to make clear is that when issues relating to the admissibility of documents are raised, they will be decided. They will be decided. Whether they will be ultimately the final -- but they will be resolved after the end of the evidentiary stage. You will know from decision to decision. The other matter that you raised was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Self-propelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The question arose before. Orphaned, self-propelled, call them whatever you like. I think you understand that there can't be a hard and fast rule that a document that has been tendered and admitted which, however, has not been used or put to any witness automatically means that it has no probative value or that the Trial Chamber should not even look at it. That has never been a rule before this Tribunal. You know it as much as I can. That document can ultimately be corroborated by other evidence, by other documents, or it could corroborate other evidence and other documents. So at the end of the day, this is the rule basically. Now, at the end of the day, of course at the end of the trial there can be submissions on what probative value should be given to any documents that have not been put to witnesses, and we will deal with -- with those issues as and when they arise. There are some legal conclusions to be drawn, obviously, because a document that has been put to a witness and questions asked and answered in relation to that witness, both as regards authenticity and as regards the contents of that witness -- of that document. And the document which has never been put to any witness, we will understand that they cannot be treated the same, but there can be other evidence that could raise the probative value of documents that are not put to any witness. This is the position, and of course we will deal with it as we go along. That's the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: With your permission, Your Honour, I would just like to make that our concern at this time is that on the Prosecution's proposed list of exhibits there are 2.100 exhibits. We anticipate that well over 500 of these documents will not be introduced through witnesses. We would just like to know from the Prosecution when and how they intend to present these documents and when and how the Trial Chamber intends to declare them as admissible. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, the ball is in your court, Mr. McCloskey, initially, and then we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As is appropriate as the trial unfolds, I hope to cut exhibits, and we have chosen our exhibits -- we've tried to choose them in a targeted way, but I still hope that I will be able to reduce that. But I think when we're talking about large numbers of exhibits, many times we're talking about documents related to some kind of expert report or forensic report or something like that. Mr. Butler's report, for example, cites all kinds of documents, and I'm certainly not going to have Mr. Butler discuss every one of those. You'd shoot me by the time I was through with that. But I have chosen a list of about -- well, it's too big right now and it's getting smaller, but 100, 200 documents and/or intercepts that Mr. Butler will discuss, but that will leave several hundred more. But that will be part of his report, cited in his report, not just floating out in the air. I hope not to have too many floating documents. They're not worth much if they're just floating out there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will be up to you, basically. We cannot interfere in the Prosecution's discretion not to tender any documents that they initially indicated as prospective exhibits, but then we'll deal with it. May I suggest something? We don't have -- unless you intend to raise other issues that would engage us for some time, we do not have on our agenda much more. Can I suggest that, rather than having a break now and reconvening in half an hour, we continue and finish, but I need the go-ahead from technicians. I can barely see behind the tinted windows. Well, of course they will need time to change tapes, et cetera, but I don't think it will last us much longer. Do you have any particular submissions that you anticipate will engage us?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There is one matter I'd like to raise which may be of some substance, I don't know yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, then we have a break. 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed. Everyone is here. We would like to raise with you a matter related to the possibility that we may have a number of Rule 92 bis witnesses come forward for cross-examination. One undesirable scenario is that the witness will enter the courtroom, sit wherever he is supposed to sit, or she is supposed to sit, and next thing that happens maybe the Prosecution has a couple of questions that they may wish to put, and then straight cross-examination, and the poor witness sometimes is almost completely unprepared, doesn't even -- it just falls on him. So our suggestion -- and actually it's not just a suggestion, this is how we plan to proceed: When a Rule 92 bis witness arrives to be cross-examined or, even before that, to be asked some additional questions by the Prosecutor, the testimony of that witness should be preceded by a short description by the party producing that witness. In this case if the witness is your witness, Mr. McCloskey, but he's being produced for cross-examination, irrespective of whether you have additional questions to that witness or not, you will be required - you or Mr. Nicholls or whoever will be with you - to make a short presentation describing the substance of the -- his 92 bis testimony, and then we can proceed with the rest. It's a measure that we mean to introduce to make it easier for the witnesses than has maybe been in the past. Tolimir. Tolimir. Tolimir, I think we put -- made our position clear last time. We would expect, unless he turns up between now and when we resume in August, we would expect to see his name eliminated from the list of the accused in this case. One other thing that sometimes causes a little bit of problems is that the general rule pertaining to the filing of motions is that motions should be filed publicly. There is no rule which envisages that they should first be filed confidentially. They should be filed publicly. If there is sensitive information or other information that needs to be filed confidentially, that will -- that information will be appended to the motion and marked as confidential but not the motion itself. The motion itself will or can be presented confidentially if there are indeed serious, justifiable reasons for doing so. There are many instances where we, of course, allow the filing of motions in a confidential manner, but the rule should be that they should be filed openly unless there are serious reasons for -- and you would be required to demonstrate good cause when you proceed with filing of a motion in a confidential manner unless it is obvious from the text of the motion itself. Before I proceed, Judge Kwon, are there any issues you would like to raise that I may have overlooked? Judge Prost? Judge Stole? Okay. Let me start with the Prosecution. I'll come to the accused later, but are there any issues that you would like to raise which we may have overlooked?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Defence teams. We'll go -- we'll make the rounds. Mr. Zivanovic for Mr. Popovic first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, I have one matter that I'd like to raise and it really relates to the Prosecution's 98 bis obligations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: 98 -- or 68, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because 98 is our obligation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I don't want to be making any allegations there, Mr. President. As I understand it, last Thursday at the Status Conference then, the Prosecution indicated that there was some further material in relation to some trials that were being conducted in Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- and Boston, and as I understand it we were going to receive some indication today as to, firstly, what the status of that material was and, obviously, secondly, when the Defence can expect to have that material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for raising the matter. I never understood the Prosecution to say that they will be providing the information today. What I understood from Mr. McCloskey last time, but of course I will soon give him the floor, that this was being considered by and actively pursued by the Office of the Prosecutor and that further disclosures will follow when the information becomes available. This is how I understood you. If I have understood you wrongly or if you have any further communication to make in relation to these pending cases outside this Tribunal, please go ahead, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That was my understanding, and we encourage counsel to come ask us directly. We'll tell you the same. I can give you a brief update. I've requested -- the case is Boston is finished. It's gone to verdict in an immigration fraud case, and Mr. Butler testified in that briefly as did, I believe at least one survivor from Branjevo farm, and I've requested the transcripts from the United States, that you get that from a court reporter and it's all hopefully within 30 days, but that goes system to system. Bosnia, I hope you'll all help us with. We talk with them. We have some summaries. We're about ready to send what information we've got from the Kravica warehouse case, and we have information about the collections that we spoke of briefly before we were able to clarify that issue about which collections we're talking about, and I can provide -- well, I might as well. The collection in Banja Luka was a new collection. It was found out based on a request for assistance of May this year for Sarajevo-Romanija Corps material for the upcoming case of Galic and Milosevic. They were shown an archive and it turned out this archive had lots of material. They were there last week and we now have a very rough outline of documents. There are several thousand documents that look like they have relevance. We haven't spotted any huge guns, smoking or cold or non-existent, but we -- I'm told that that material will be indexed and ERN'd within three weeks and we'll get to the Defence. But that's new material. There's been a few other false alarms, I believe, of various disks of other material about the 28th Division, and we've looked at it and it looks like it's mostly stuff we've had before. So that's the update on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that statement, Mr. McCloskey. The position, Ms. Condon, is that here in this Tribunal the Rule 68 disclosure process is an ongoing process, and you will find out that throughout the trial itself there will be several instances where you will be receiving fresh documents which are disclosed under Rule 68. The reason why they are disclosed in the course of the trial and not prior to the trial is that sometimes they are not immediately identified as Rule 68 material, sometimes they become available after the start of the trial, sometimes they are here for quite some time but they form part of a large collection that has to be vetted. So the important thing is that the Prosecution attends to their obligation of disclosure well, as required by the Rule, failing which, of course, we will have problems. It's as simple as that. I mean, what we should be all avoiding is the situation where all of a sudden we come here and we say, ah, this has just been disclosed to us and we have found out that the Prosecution had it since 1997, for example, in its archive. So we'll play it by the ear as we go along, but my experience here has been that the Prosecution does not normally avoid or try to evade its -- or their responsibility under Rule 68. But of course these issues, the particular instances that you have raised, I think trust Mr. McCloskey and then we will see. If we have reason to be strict with the Prosecutor, then we will do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I won't make any comment about trusting Prosecutors, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey, any comment on that? Mr. Ostojic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would prefer her to come by me before she makes statements. And statements that are going to go to my integrity, I don't appreciate jokes either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Ostojic, would you like to raise any other matter that we have not dealt with?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. None at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you solved your problems with the e-mail -- Tribunal e-mail system?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have not yet, Your Honour, but we're working towards that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is the problem, if I may ask, because you've been here, appearing on other trials. You're not a newcomer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't know, and if we knew, then we would solve the problem. We tried this afternoon to resolve it. We're unsuccessful and we're sill trying and we have scheduled a meeting after this conference to meet again to resolve it. I'm just not sure why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Basically, I don't have any outstanding issues, but I would just like to indicate that in the transcript it says Mr. Stojanovic instead of Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for pointing that out. So I suppose that will be corrected in due course. Madam Ivanovic or Madam Faveau, whichever you prefer, would you like to raise any other matter, or for that matter, any issue that you would like us to make guidelines or come down with guidelines that we have not dealt with already?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that you have covered all the important subjects so far, but I would like to draw your attention to a press communique that was issued from the press service of this Tribunal. It's a second communique because there was a first one in July according to which the seven accused were accused of genocide. Today a new press communique was issued and we can read the following in this press communique: [Previous translation continued ...] "[In English] ... trial in which seven senior Bosnian Serb military officials are charged with genocide." [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm quite sure that you will understand the subject of my concern. The Tribunal is giving a certain image of this trial and of itself, and I believe that the information that comes out of this Tribunal should be as precise as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I couldn't agree more with you, Madam Ivanovic. I haven't seen the press release. I will have a look at it, together with the other two Judges, and we'll address the matter if at all necessary. Yes. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We don't have any outstanding issue for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, previously you said you would like to raise a matter, an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We're really seeking the guidance and assistance of the Trial Chamber and perhaps -- well, certainly the Prosecution as well. We all like to come to these hearings as well prepared as is possible to help you resolve the issues that arise, and it's fair to say, and I think Ms. Fauveau has already said this, we really haven't left a stone unturned this afternoon. I've kept a very careful catalogue of the issues that we have dealt with. I dare say you will correct me if I'm wrong, but I think we've only left two items on the agenda over until tomorrow. As far as I understand the position tomorrow, and indeed I think as far as all of the Defence understand the position tomorrow, there will be no opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And there appears to be very little left for us to deal with tomorrow in the morning, and so it's something of an intrigue that this Court has set aside no less than nine hours of court time for what appears to be a fairly formal procedure, and I would like to know, and I know all my colleagues would like to know from the Chamber and from the Prosecution what is on the agenda tomorrow so that we can be properly prepared for it. And that's really the issue I want to raise at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you so much, Mr. Haynes, and precisely we were coming to that towards the end. The idea of having a sitting scheduled for the morning and another sitting scheduled for the afternoon does not originate from us. It originates from the Registry, and I tried to find out what was the reason behind it, and the reason behind it was that they anticipated possibly the need or the eventuality that we might require to have an afternoon sitting as well. We had not asked for two sittings in one day, but that's how it happened. You can take it for granted that there will be, especially since there are no spillovers from this Pre-Trial Conference to tomorrow, that there will only be a morning sitting and no sitting in the afternoon. That was, I understand, a measure taken by the Registry ex abundantia. So that, I think, knocks off the afternoon sitting. The morning sitting, yes, there is agreement amongst all of us that although tomorrow will be the kick-off, there will not be opening statements for reasons that have been, in a transparent manner, discussed and agreed upon going back to February, I think -- to April. In April we had already decided when the opening statements would occur. We also decided that the case was presented -- is huge and presented so many aspects to be taken into account before we really start with the evidentiary stage that it was important to have both the Ad Litem Judge and the Reserve Ad Litem Judge in place here in good timely fashion to enable them to sit down and become familiar with the details of the case and also give an opportunity to start training in the e-court system, which you will have an occasion, as I said. So what is going to happen tomorrow? Tomorrow we will try to distill and condense today's discussion and agreement in relation to guidelines. No guidelines on the usual hearsay or the usual -- I mean, that stuff you know, but we will come down tomorrow with a decision that we are already working upon which will define certain -- certain guidelines that will become applicable in the course of this trial. We will give you also a clear indication as to how we intend to proceed in matters relating to examination-in-chief, cross-examination, along the lines that we have discussed earlier. I understand from what I have been told that although there will be no opening statements tomorrow, Madam Prosecutor is turning up and she would like to give some information to the Trial Chamber. I haven't got a clue what it is about. We'll see tomorrow. We also have -- the other issue was we'll probably decide orally again tomorrow Beara's motion for leave and a few other things, but basically that's it. Tomorrow we kick off. I don't think there are any -- there should be any concerns as to whether there will be any surprises that you would be unprepared -- unprepared for. But starting tomorrow has solved a lot of problems for the Trial Chamber, and it has also, I think, created an environment which should send you home for your summer recess with sufficient time to prepare yourself better. Yes. There is -- yes. And we will also deal with the protective measures issue tomorrow, tomorrow morning. There's one final issue that I would rather deal with now. If you prefer to come forward with a response tomorrow, I think that is fair enough. The thing is how are we going to proceed. This is by no means an easy case. It's also a case that is going to last a considerable time. It is a case where there are plenty of us in one courtroom. We intend to sit on a five-day basis. That's Monday to Friday. But we all have had sufficient trial experience here in this Tribunal to know that there comes a time when Prosecution needs some time to reorganise itself, Defence teams have been inundated with an influx of piles if not sometimes hundreds or thousands of new documents and time is needed to go through these documents. We may establish a pattern beforehand, but before we establish a pattern as regards sittings and breaks, we would like you, like you have been doing so far in the spirit of cooperation, to sit together first, Prosecution and Defence teams, and see if you can come to an agreement and make a concrete suggestion to Trial Chamber. Trial Chamber then will obviously consider whether it's in the best interests of justice to grant your wishes or whether to propose something different or to deal with the issue as we go along. But we want to make sure that we don't get to a stage where everyone has been overworked or where everyone is overtired, because that would lead to confrontation, it would lead to attrition sometimes, and we have got every intention to make sure that each one of you is and continues to be working in an environment that is conducive to good management of this trial. So what I suggest is that if there is anything else that needs to be addressed now, that we adjourn on this note and then you come forward tomorrow with some proposals. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm sorry to enforce this upon Your Honour and indeed everybody else in court, but I can't accede to the suggestion that we adjourn now. You have touched upon the very thing that concerns us. We were all intrigued by an item which arose from a press briefing dated the 21st of June which indicated that we were to expect Ms. Del Ponte here tomorrow to deliver a statement, and to quote the press briefing, "Which will be more than procedural and is expected to be of great interest." Like Your Honour, we have no idea what she proposes to say, and we wondered as a first step whether anybody could give us some idea what she proposes to say. Our primary position is that such a statement has absolutely no place in tomorrow's proceedings. Tomorrow will be the formal opening of the trial against these seven accused, the start of trial proceedings that require careful regulation and ought, in our submission, to be limited to admissible evidence and proper argument thereupon. The regulation of those proceedings is a matter for Your Honour. In simple terms, this is your court, not Mrs. Del Ponte's. If Mrs. Del Ponte wishes to make interesting statements or announcements for the benefit of the world's media, she has access to perfectly adequate facilities, both inside this building, outside this building, and elsewhere. And I'm sorry, at quarter to 7.00 in the evening, but I'm going to invite you to make a decision about whether any such statement can properly be made tomorrow at the formal opening of the trial against these seven accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we are in the same unfortunate position as you are. We don't know what kind of statement to expect. So, Mr. McCloskey, are you in a position to enlighten us on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe as the formal opening, as you've designated, she wanted to say a few words about the importance of the case. Five minutes maybe, maybe six to eight. Something that I may -- could say myself. She's the Prosecutor. The formal opening of the case, how important this case is, and perhaps direct your attention to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it's a part of opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It could be viewed that way. It could be viewed as a ceremonial statement as part of the formal opening, as it's been designated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Introduction to your opening statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's very similar to what I said in my opening statement or what Mark Harmon said in his opening statement before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To my understanding, this has happened before. It happened in Prlic, I think. In Prlic I think she was even invited by the Trial Chamber to be there and make a statement or something like that. I don't know exactly what happened. I can check. But I know that she made a statement in Prlic. Let's do it this way, because not knowing what the plans are, what her intentions are, how can ask even --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can I invite you? My primary submission is that you should simply disallow any statement being made tomorrow. It's inappropriate and it's not a proper part of tomorrow's proceedings. But if you're prepared to countenance the making of such a statement by Mrs. Del Ponte, I'm going to ask you to make four directions: Firstly, that as precise as possible a text of that address to the Court tomorrow is made available within 30 minutes. Secondly, that no address be received from her until at least 12.00 noon. That would enable at least one of the counsel in each team to go to the Detention Unit tomorrow morning and take their client's instructions on their reaction to such a statement. Thirdly, that prior to any such statement being heard by the Trial Chamber and the public, that there should be discussion and argument as to the propriety of the making of such a statement in whole or in part in private session. And fourthly, if you are going to permit such a statement to be made, that each of the accused has the right to respond to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think you will not have any comment from me on this until I have thoroughly discussed it with the -- the Judges, and again, what I suggest is that we move this to tomorrow morning because there is no way we can hand down decision on this this evening by 7.00, and we cannot keep anyone else here beyond 7.00. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if counsel could enlighten on us on what authority he is citing to such -- does he intend to find out what I intend say before each day of the court? What's the purpose of this? Where's the prejudice? A Prosecutor is saying how important her case is. This is being built into some grand issue which really there's no -- not one citation to any law or authority nor any citation of anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I've only just been told she's going to speak tomorrow. So you'll forgive me if I haven't been able to look up authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, let's establish this straight away: No cross --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's one unwritten rule that you need to observe all the time. Please address the Trial Chamber and not each other. That's first, and I hope the last time I will need to say that, to state that. I think we need to retire, withdraw, discuss this amongst ourselves, and then tomorrow morning we will -- if we need to discuss it further, we will discuss it further, and then we'll take a decision. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We did not have the opportunity to say whether there was other issues we wanted to raise. There are two such issues but I will, with your permission, keep them for tomorrow. They're not critical issues which must be handled at this time. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, shall we ask Mr. Bourgon to provide you with at least 30-minutes advanced notice so we can -- yes, Mr. Bourgon. Can we at least know what they are?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: They are two quick issues, Mr. President. The first one deals with an issue that we raise in our pre-trial brief which regards Prosecution's pre-trial brief and defects in that document, that we have problems working with that document. The second issue deals with the order of the names of the accused on the indictment further to your decision that was rendered this morning. You basically ordered that paragraph 65(E)(vi) in which order the names of the accused would appear, and I would like to make submissions in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So the understanding is we will reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00. If we need to discuss further with you the matter relating to Madam Del Ponte's intended intervention, we'll do that. Otherwise, we'll just come down with a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was surprised to hear you say that you were not asked whether you had other matters to raise. I have been doing the round whether you have other matters you would like to raise. I asked Madam Nikolic. Really?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My apologies to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was quite by accident that you failed to mention us, but thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any further -- yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps we should think about -- a rule about two counsel for each side and they seem to be popping up one after another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think as we go along the rule that will be observed here is the rule that is observed worldwide: If there are two, three counsel for an accused, it should be one counsel that should deal with any particular matter and not -- not both. But again, there may be instances where we would allow for exceptions. Sometimes it becomes necessary. But the rule is, as we all know it here, that if there are two, it's only one that should speak or intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We shall adjourn. I would like to thank the interpreters, the technicians, and our staff and all the others that have made it possible to conduct this Pre-Trial Conference. Tomorrow, we will continue with a few remaining issues and then move to the opening of the trial. Thank you, and good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: adjourned at 6.55 p.m.
